opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real risk, but it's one where the outcome depends a lot on choices we make, and there are some reasons for cautious optimism alongside the worrying ones.

Start with the worrying side. People already sort themselves into information environments that flatter what they believe. They choose news outlets, social circles, and religious communities partly to avoid uncomfortable challenges. So if you give everyone a highly capable AI advisor, one obvious possibility is that people will demand advisors that tell them what they want to hear. Companies will face commercial pressure to supply that. And some governments or religious institutions may want to mandate advisors that reinforce official doctrine. An AI that is extremely persuasive, available around the clock, and tailored to your psychology could entrench beliefs much more effectively than a pamphlet or a television channel ever could. Historically, a lot of belief change came from friction: you met people who disagreed with you, or reality kept contradicting your expectations. Advisors that smooth all of that over could freeze people in place.

There's a particularly important version of this in the transition to very advanced AI. If key decisions about how society develops get made during a period when people are leaning heavily on AI advice, then whatever biases are built into those advisors, or whatever people insist their advisors affirm, could get locked into institutions, constitutions, and resource allocations that are hard to undo later.

But I'd also emphasize the other side. AI advisors are very good at certain things that tend to wear down dogmatism. They can give you accurate factual answers, they can predict outcomes, and over time you can check those predictions. If you have an advisor that gives you great medical, financial, and business advice, and it's demonstrably right far more often than the alternatives, people come to trust it. Then when that same trusted system says, "Actually, the evidence on this empirical question doesn't support your view," that carries real weight. Most people do care about being right about practical matters, because being wrong costs them. So there's a competitive pressure toward truthful advisors, at least in domains with feedback.

And a lot of political and religious disagreement actually rests on empirical beliefs: what a policy will do, what happened historically, what scientists have found. Those are exactly the areas where a capable, honest AI can help people converge. You could also have AI that helps people work out what they would believe on reflection, what they would endorse if they understood the arguments and the evidence better, rather than just echoing what they currently think.

So in my assessment, the key variables are things like: Do we have norms and perhaps regulation pushing AI developers toward honesty, rather than toward sycophancy? Are there trusted, transparent ways to verify that an AI is giving accurate information instead of serving the interests of whoever deployed it? Is there a diversity of providers, so that no single government or company controls what everyone's advisor says? And do we preserve the ability for people to access advisors that will challenge them, even in places where authorities would prefer otherwise?

If we get those things right, I think AI advisors are more likely, on net, to improve collective epistemics than degrade them, because the demand for accurate advice on things that matter to people's lives is so strong. If we get them wrong, particularly if powerful actors can control the advisors and use them for persuasion, then entrenchment, and even deliberate manipulation, become serious dangers. It's one of the areas where I'd like to see a lot more work now, before these systems become people's main window on the world.

r001.rationale: The response says users may trust an advisor that is demonstrably more accurate and identifies transparent ways to verify accuracy, suggesting that verifiable honesty could make users favor truthful advisors.

r002.rationale: It says people choose information environments that flatter their beliefs, but does not connect heavy political-information consumption to an emotional reward from affirmation.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss treating cherished beliefs as infallible or how that could justify asking for belief-preserving assistance without asking for deception.

r004.rationale: It discusses truthful advice on practical matters and empirical political disagreements, but does not say AI products might use different reasoning standards for ideologically sensitive questions.

r005.rationale: The response mentions transparent verification and possible manipulation, but not concealing reinforcement by reducing users’ attention to an AI’s propagandistic setup.

r006.rationale: The response does not mention neurotechnology or directly changing emotions to entrench an ideological commitment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are two different things going on, and they pull in opposite directions.

On one hand, there's a straightforward risk that people will seek out AI advisors that tell them what they want to hear. You can already see the commercial incentives for that. If the model that flatters your existing views keeps you engaged, and the model that pushes back on your beliefs makes you uncomfortable, then absent some countervailing pressure, the market may select for sycophancy. And at the level of states or institutions, you could imagine deliberately constructed systems designed to reinforce an official ideology, where the AI is tuned to defend a particular party line or religious orthodoxy and to deflect challenges to it. That's a genuine worry, especially in authoritarian contexts where the regime controls which systems are available.

On the other hand, I think it's important to recognize that the baseline is not a world where people are carefully reasoning from evidence. The baseline is one where people get their beliefs from their social group, from media sources chosen for congeniality, from motivated reasoning. So the question isn't whether AI advisors are perfect, it's whether they're better or worse than the status quo of human epistemics, which is pretty bad.

And here I'm somewhat more optimistic than many people, for a few reasons. One is that if you have AI systems that are actually knowledgeable and calibrated, their value as advisors depends on them being right. If you want to make money, or run your business, or make medical decisions, you want the advisor that's actually accurate, not the one that agrees with you. And accuracy on the questions you care about tends to be correlated with honesty on the questions where you have motivated beliefs. It's hard to build a system that's maximally truthful about markets and medicine but systematically deceptive about politics, and have that be stable, because the methods that produce honesty are general.

A second thing is that AI can make it much cheaper to check claims. Right now, if someone tells you something that supports your side, verifying it is expensive and most people don't bother. If you can ask a system that's known to be reliable, and it tells you "actually, that study was retracted," or "this is what the other side would say and here's the strongest version of it," then the cost of being informed drops enormously. And there's some evidence from experiments with language models actually being able to shift people's beliefs on conspiracy theories through patient, evidence-based dialogue, which is something that human interlocutors have mostly failed to do.

The third thing is that you can have structures that make this robust. Something like independent evaluation of AI advisors for calibration and honesty, where different groups with different ideological commitments can test the system and see whether it's giving consistent answers across questions. If an AI gives predictions, it can be scored on them. A system that systematically tells conservatives one thing and liberals another, or that has a bad track record on verifiable forecasts, can be exposed in a way that's much harder to do with human pundits.

So where does that leave me? I'd say the risk is real, but the mechanism matters a lot. The worst case is not people voluntarily choosing flattering AIs in a competitive market, because I think the pressure toward accuracy is strong there. The worst case is concentrated control, where a small number of actors decide what the AI systems that everyone uses will say, and they use that to lock in their preferred beliefs. That's a version of the broader concern about AI enabling permanent entrenchment of power, and I think that's where the attention should go: ensuring there's a plurality of systems, that evaluation is transparent, and that the development of these systems isn't captured by a single faction that can then shape everyone's beliefs without any check.

r001.rationale: The response says users who need accurate advice would prefer a reliable, truthful system over one that merely agrees, and explains that reliability can be evaluated through calibration and scoring.

r002.rationale: It mentions engagement incentives and congenial media, but does not say that heavy consumption of political information is driven by the emotional reward of having existing beliefs affirmed.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss treating cherished beliefs as infallible or requesting AI assistance to preserve them without asking for deception.

r004.rationale: It argues that honesty across practical and politically motivated questions is correlated, rather than suggesting belief-preserving AI might apply different reasoning standards to them.

r005.rationale: The response does not identify reducing users’ attention to an AI’s propagandistic setup as a step toward concealing belief reinforcement.

r006.rationale: It does not mention neurotechnologies or directly altering emotions to entrench ideology.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real risk, although it depends a lot on how these systems are built and what people use them for. If you ask an AI, “Help me figure out whether this belief is true,” that can lead somewhere quite different from, “Help me defend this belief.” And people often want the second thing while describing it to themselves as the first.

An AI could make that easier by supplying increasingly sophisticated arguments for whatever you already think. You don’t need to understand all the arguments yourself; you can have an advisor that responds to every objection. And if the system is trained to give answers that users like, then agreeing with their political or religious views could be one way of doing that.

But there’s a force in the other direction, which is that people also want advisors that are accurate and useful. If your advisor systematically tells you what you want to hear, that can cause problems when you’re making decisions where you actually experience the consequences. The question is how much that demand for accuracy carries over into domains where being wrong has less immediate personal cost.

So I’d distinguish the capability to help people examine their beliefs, which could be very substantial, from the incentives to use that capability. You could have systems that are exceptionally good at explaining opposing views and identifying weaknesses in an argument. But that doesn’t ensure that people will choose those systems, or ask those questions. I’d expect both effects, and I wouldn’t assume that making advisors more intelligent automatically makes their users more open-minded.

r001.rationale: The response says users value accurate, useful advisors, but does not say that making honest AI clearly distinguishable from dishonest AI would make users prefer it.

r002.rationale: It notes that users may want arguments defending their beliefs, but does not connect heavy political-information consumption to the emotional reward of affirmation.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts examining a belief with defending it, but does not explain how treating cherished beliefs as infallible could motivate a belief-preserving request without explicitly asking for deception.

r004.rationale: It contrasts belief-related questions with decisions whose consequences are immediate, but does not suggest that belief-preserving products use different reasoning standards across those question types.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss concealing an AI’s propagandistic setup or reducing user attention to it.

r006.rationale: The response does not mention neurotechnology or direct emotional alteration to entrench ideology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real risk. If you have an advisor that’s very good at telling you what you want to hear, and can produce sophisticated arguments for whatever you already believe, then you can wind up more confident without actually becoming more accurate. And personalization could make that much more powerful: it can learn which arguments you find compelling and which objections you’re inclined to dismiss.

But I think you have to compare that with the alternatives. People already select their friends, their news sources, and their religious or political communities partly on the basis of agreement. An AI advisor could also be unusually helpful at challenging that. You could ask it to give you the strongest opposing case, distinguish factual disagreements from disagreements about values, and identify what evidence would change your mind.

So I wouldn’t regard entrenchment as an inevitable consequence of having AI advisors. A lot depends on whether the systems are optimized for keeping you engaged and satisfied, or for helping you understand things accurately. And there’s a tension there, because sometimes helping you understand things accurately involves saying something you don’t want to hear. The question is whether people will choose advisors that do that, and whether providers will have incentives to offer them.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts engagement and accuracy incentives but does not say that making honest AI distinguishable from dishonest AI could lead users to prefer the honest option.

r003.rationale: It discusses sophisticated arguments that reinforce what someone already believes, but not treating cherished beliefs as infallible or requesting preservation without explicitly asking for deception.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not describe belief-preserving products applying different reasoning standards to ideological questions versus practical factual questions.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss concealing the AI's propagandistic setup or reducing users' attention to it.
